newsitem.title: UK: Irish premier calls for patience on N. Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Irish premier calls for patience on N. Ireland.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton called on Thursday for patience in the Northern Irish peace process as Catholics and Protestants clamoured for a public response from Britain to a republican ceasefire plan.

Bruton is due to meet British Prime Minister John Major in London on December 9 to discuss the flagging peace process after Catholic leaders offered a set of terms in exchange for a new ceasefire by the Irish Republican Army (IRA).
Major effectively spurned the proposals earlier this week when he said he was not prepared to alter his policy on Northern Ireland.

But Irish leaders have sought to smooth over the apparent rejection, saying talks to try to get a new IRA ceasefire and to bring republican leaders into talks on the future of the province were still underway.
"It is important that this time we have to be as careful as possible in laying the grounds for the next step so there won't be any misunderstanding after the event," Bruton told the BBC.
"Therefore we have to be as patient as possible."
The IRA abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February with the first of a series of bombings in its renewed campaign for a united Ireland.
The guerrillas have not carried out any attacks for nearly two months, raising speculation that they are operating an unofficial truce to try to win concessions for Sinn Fein, their political wing.
Sinn Fein is barred from the Northern Ireland talks, jointly sponsored by Britain and Ireland, because of the guerrillas' refusal to call a new truce.

Pro-British "Loyalist" leaders suspect Britain has been doing secret deals with the republicans and have called on Major to publish his response to the proposals set out by Sinn Fein and John Hume, leader of the moderate Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party.

"As an elected representative of the Ulster people I am going to demand to see what he (Major) is negotiating and talking about," said Ian Paisley, leader of the hardline pro-British Democratic Unionist Party.

Media reports say Major has written to Hume setting out his response to the plan, under which Sinn Fein would be allowed into talks almost immediately after the IRA called a truce and demands that the guerrillas dispose of their arms be dropped.
Hume has accused Major of rejecting the proposals for fear of offending the unionists on whom he relies to bolster his majority of just one in the British parliament.
The unionists usually vote with the government but they have threatened to withdraw their cooperation if Major grants any concessions to the republicans.
Loyalist leaders are taking part in the peace talks because their guerrillas are still honouring a two year truce in their war to keep Northern Ireland under British rule.
Irish leaders say a Christmas recess in the peace talks would provide Britain with an ideal opportunity to test an IRA ceasefire before allowing Sinn Fein to take part in January.
